summary: The talk begins with an overview of RAG implementations ranging from naive three-step pipelines to advanced versions with query expansion, reranking, and fusion, through to agentic RAG with query routing and self-improvement. Qdrant is introduced as an open-source Rust-based vector search database for generative AI at scale. Atita enumerates challenges across every pipeline stage: data extraction failures, chunking and embedding model selection, retrieval relevance and ordering, response accuracy, context adherence, and scaling. Numerous improvement techniques are presented for each stage, including data cleaning, domain-specific embedding models, metadata filtering, semantic chunking, indexing algorithms (HNSW, BM25, graphs), document reranking, chain-of-thought prompting, and dense/sparse vector combinations. Deanna then introduces Quotient AI's evaluation platform, which generates realistic evaluation datasets and handles prompt formatting, LLM execution, and metric computation. A demo builds RAG for Qdrant documentation QA, optimizing for faithfulness alongside context relevance, chunk relevance, and text quality. The first five experiments adjust chunk size, retrieval window, embedding models, and LLM choice, with smaller chunks plus a larger retrieval window achieving the best results and GPT-3.5 improving all metrics. High variance in context relevance prompts deeper analysis of the two worst-performing data points, revealing the system over-indexes on common terms like 'quadrant support and search.' Three reranking experiments using MixedBread, Cohere, and Jina's ColBERT model improve context relevance and faithfulness, with Cohere performing best. However, some questions remain poorly served, suggesting domain-specific terminology limits generic embedding models. Two hybrid search implementations (sparse plus dense vectors, with and without a ranker) are then tested; Cohere ranker with hybrid search achieves the best performance across all metrics except chunk relevance, resolving both worst-performing data points. Over ten experiments, faithfulness improves from 76 to just under 85 without changing the generic QA prompt. The speakers conclude that there is no substitute for evaluation-based, data-driven improvement, leveraging domain understanding, keeping evaluation datasets current, and avoiding over-engineering without carefully chosen metric combinations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: RAG implementations range from naive to agentic, with vector databases common to all and challenges spanning every pipeline stage.
Many improvement levers exist—data cleaning, semantic chunking, metadata filtering, reranking, hybrid search, embedding/LLM selection—making evaluation essential for knowing what to change.
Quotient AI generates evaluation datasets and orchestrates prompt formatting, LLM execution, and metric computation for systematic RAG experimentation.
Key metrics—context relevance, chunk relevance, faithfulness, and text quality—must be combined to diagnose underlying issues and guide iteration.
Smaller chunk size with a larger retrieval window outperformed simply increasing chunk size, achieving the best relevance and faithfulness in early experiments.

Reranking with Cohere improved context relevance and faithfulness over naive RAG, and combining hybrid search (sparse + dense vectors) with the Cohere ranker achieved the best overall performance across all metrics except chunk relevance.
Domain-specific terminology in documentation limits generic embedding models; hybrid search with sparse vectors helps capture similar terminology.
Over ten experiments, faithfulness improved from 76 to just under 85 without changing the generic QA prompt, demonstrating incremental evaluation-driven optimization.
There is no substitute for evaluation-based, data-driven improvements; keep evaluation datasets current and avoid over-engineering without carefully chosen metric combinations.
Identify common failure points across the RAG pipeline from data processing through response generation.

sections.title: Introduction and RAG Overview
sections.summary: Atita and Deanna introduce themselves and outline the talk on RAG optimization. They define RAG as combining search/retrieval from a knowledge source (usually a vector database) with LLM generation, and preview discussion of challenges and evaluation-based optimization techniques.

sections.title: RAG Implementation Types and Qdrant
sections.summary: Atita describes naive, advanced, and agentic RAG implementations, noting that a vector database is common to all. She introduces Qdrant as an open-source Rust-based vector search database for generative AI at scale, emphasizing retrieval performance, scalability, and resource optimization.

sections.title: RAG Challenges Across Pipeline Stages
sections.summary: Challenges are mapped to each pipeline stage: data processing (missing/incorrectly extracted info), data ingestion (chunking strategy, embedding model selection), retrieval (relevance, retrieval window, document ordering), and response generation (incorrect/incomplete answers, context straying, ambiguous queries, scaling, security).

sections.title: Improvement Techniques for RAG
sections.summary: Atita enumerates improvement techniques: data cleaning, advanced extraction, domain-specific embedding models, metadata filtering, chunking strategy refinement (semantic chunking, reducing chunk size), appropriate context sizing, indexing algorithms (HNSW, BM25, graphs), document reranking, chain-of-thought prompting, dense and sparse vector combinations, LLM experimentation, and task-specific agents.

sections.title: Evaluation Motivation and Quotient Introduction
sections.summary: With many levers to tweak, evaluation is essential for measuring progress and making informed decisions. Deanna introduces Quotient AI's evaluation solution, which provides realistic evaluation datasets (or generates them), handles prompt formatting, LLM execution, and metric computation for iterative RAG optimization.

sections.title: Demo: RAG Evaluation Workflow and Metrics
sections.summary: Deanna presents a demo building RAG for Qdrant documentation QA, optimizing for faithfulness (minimizing hallucinations). Metrics include context relevance, chunk relevance, faithfulness, and text quality. Five experiments are run: baseline, increased chunk size (dropped faithfulness), smaller chunks + larger retrieval window (best results), new embedding model (no improvement), and GPT-3.5 LLM switch (improved all metrics). High variance in context relevance is noted.

sections.title: Advanced RAG: Reranking, Hybrid Search, and Conclusions
sections.summary: Analysis of the two worst-performing data points reveals the system over-indexes on common terms like 'quadrant support and search.' Three reranking experiments (MixedBread, Cohere, Jina ColBERT) improve context relevance and faithfulness, with Cohere best. Domain-specific terminology limits generic embeddings, motivating hybrid search (sparse + dense vectors). Cohere ranker with hybrid search achieves best performance across all metrics except chunk relevance, resolving both worst data points. Over ten experiments, faithfulness improved from 76 to just under 85 without changing the QA prompt. The speakers conclude emphasizing evaluation-based, data-driven improvement, domain understanding, keeping evaluation datasets current, and avoiding over-engineering.

demonstrations: Notebook demo building a RAG QA system on Qdrant documentation, pre-executed and available on GitHub via QR code.

Ten-iteration experiment series: baseline naive RAG, increased chunk size, smaller chunk + larger retrieval window, new embedding model, GPT-3.5 LLM switch, three reranking experiments (MixedBread, Cohere, Jina ColBERT), and two hybrid search implementations (with and without Cohere ranker).
Quotient platform workflow: populate evaluation dataset by querying Qdrant for contexts, then submit to Quotient for orchestration and metric computation.
Deep-dive analysis of the two worst-performing data points to diagnose over-indexing on common query terms.
limitations: Relevancy in information retrieval remains an unsolved problem even after 17 years in the field.
RAG faces persistent challenges including hallucination, incomplete responses, ambiguous queries, scaling, and data security/compliance.
With many tunable levers it is hard to know what is going wrong, what to change, and where to start without evaluation.
Generic embedding models are limited on domain-specific terminology, jargon, and acronyms; fine-tuning or training custom models is time-consuming and costly.
Expanding retrieval windows adds noise to context, potentially hurting performance.
Demo notebook was pre-executed due to time constraints; only code outputs were walked through.
quantitativeClaims: Increasing chunk size produced minor text quality improvements but a considerable drop in faithfulness.
Smaller chunk size with larger retrieval window achieved the highest relevance scores and best faithfulness score among early experiments.
Embedding model change alone did not improve performance.
LLM switch to GPT-3.5 improved performance across all metrics with the same RAG configuration.
Reranking with Cohere achieved the best relevance and faithfulness scores among three reranker experiments (MixedBread, Cohere, Jina ColBERT).
Cohere ranker combined with hybrid search achieved the best performance across all metrics except chunk relevance.
Faithfulness improved from 76 to just under 85 over ten experiments without changing the generic QA prompt.
Large variance observed in context relevance across aggregated top-performing configuration results.
